newsitem.title: USA: Major players in Oklahoma bombing trial.
newsitem.headline: Major players in Oklahoma bombing trial.

text.p: Following are the major players in the Oklahoma City bombing trial, which went to the jury on Friday.
THE DEFENDANT

-- Timothy McVeigh, a 29-year-old decorated Gulf War veteran with the looks of an "All-American boy." The Bronze Star winner is charged with making and setting off a massive truck bomb that destroyed the Oklahoma City federal building, killing 168 people and injuring 500.

The prosecution contended McVeigh, lost in a fantasy world of "Star Wars" and a hate-filled racist tract called "The Turner Diaries," wanted revenge for the government's 1993 siege at the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas, where 80 people died. The event became a rallying cry for extreme rightwingers and the government said McVeigh hoped his attack would trigger a "Second American Revolution."

McVeigh left the Army in 1991 after failing to get into the elite Special Forces and returned to his native New York, working as a security guard in Buffalo. He became a drifter, working odd jobs and selling guns.

In pre-trial interviews, McVeigh accused the government and the press of "demonizing him" and promised to take the witness stand in his own defence and answer questions about where he was on the day of the bombing, but never did.
A co-defendant, Terry Nichols, will be tried separately.
THE JUDGE

-- Lawyers call Federal Judge Richard Matsch, 66, the "Anti-Ito," a reference to Lance Ito, the judge in the O.J. Simpson criminal trial who let the case drag on and turn into a media circus. Appointed to the federal bench in 1974 by President Richard Nixon, Matsch is a jurist in total control of his court. He refused to let lawyers discuss the case out of court and maintained strict discipline inside. Known both for his quick wit and sharp rebukes of lawyers.

He was assigned to the bombing case after an appeals court disqualified an Oklahoma City judge. Matsch ruled the defendant could not get a fair trial in Oklahoma and moved the case to Denver. Born Burlington, Iowa.
LAWYERS

-- Joseph Hartzler, 46, lead prosecutor for the government, has spent all but four years of his legal career as a Justice Department attorney. He obtained convictions in Chicago for seditious conspiracy of four terrorists who sought independence for Puerto Rico.

Hartzler, picked by Attorney General Janet Reno to oversee the bombing case, graduated first in his law school class at American University. Diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 1989 and uses a motorized scooter. Born in Columbus, Ohio.

-- Stephen Jones, 56, McVeigh's lead attorney, has represented other unpopular defendants and causes in 31 years practicing law, handling 25 death-penalty cases. Served four years as general counsel of the American Civil Liberties Union Oklahoma affiliate. A Republican, he ran unsuccessfully for U.S. Senate and Oklahoma attorney general. Worked as a researcher for President Nixon in 1960s. Born Lafayette, La.
WITNESSES

-- Michael Fortier, a key witness for the prosecution, provided some of the most damning testimony of the trial, describing how McVeigh's fury at the 1993 confrontation between federal agents and Branch Davidian cult members at Waco, Texas, led him to plot an attack on the Alfred P. Murrah federal building. Fortier, 28, said McVeigh singled out the Oklahoma City federal building for the bombing "because that was where the order for the attack on Waco had come from."

He said McVeigh wanted to "cause a general uprising," to "knock some people off the fence" and push them into action against the government. An army friend of McVeigh's, he came under blistering cross-examination, admitting taking illegal drugs and bragging he would sell his story. Has pleaded guilty to four felony accounts, facing up to 23 years in prison.
-- Lori Fortier, Michael Fortier's wife, testified McVeigh illustrated how he would build the bomb by using Campbell's soup cans on the floor of her trailer in Kingman, Arizona.
Said she helped McVeigh make a fake driver's license he allegedly used to rent the truck for the bombing.

She said she did not try to dissuade McVeigh because she did not believe he was capable of the bombing. Her husband's agreement to testify in exchange for a lesser charge allowed her to escape prosecution.

-- Frederic Whitehurst, a whistleblower in the FBI testified for the defence that he found several contaminated spots in the explosives residue section of the FBI's crime lab. The charge appeared to bolster defence claims that sloppy FBI procedures may have contaminated evidence, making it unreliable. But Whitehurst also said he knew of no actual contamination of any of the evidence.
